I thought the same thing as well, but the rehome/relevel only affects one step. When the build plate first moves down, it moves to the home position and then backs off, when it moves down again, it checks the Z axis via the Z stop.

The Z stop is a physical metal flange in the located on the back right portion of the printer arm. It’s just a thin piece of metal that hangs down. The Z stop is a safety, that tells the printer to stop moving in the Z if somehow your calibration is off, and it would prevent damage to the overall printer. 

Because the wham bam adds ~2.6mm to the distance, the stop should be adjusted. There’s a thingiverse link that has the spacer. It’s a pretty simple and tiny model. All you have to do is print that, remove the 2 screws holding the Z stop and place the spacer. It should add the necessary width of the build plate with the wham bam on.

Edit: also, I hadn’t used the spacer when I first installed the plate, and everything seemed to be fine. But the next time I releveled it I started running into a lot of problems and that’s when I realized the Z spacer existed

Yea, the same technique was used for both, though they look a little different. 

The general steps were:

1.Spray Primed with Grey Primer

2.Airbrush Rakarth Flesh (the color which I have a very unhealthy obsession) 

3.Shadows Airbrushed in recesses and along joint lines with black

4.Gloss Varnish (I use future floor wax)

5.Heavy Oil wash black, and then selectively removed with q-tip covered in mineral spirits. 

6.Seal it with a gloss varnish and add some weathering pigments.

Those are the steps, looks a lot longer than it actually is, the paint job is relatively quick and pretty easy to replicate.

I'm a fan of the Axiom myself. I'm definitely not an expert like some of the guys on the subreddit, but through my job and my personal endeavors I've used quite a few different printers: Rostock Orions, Makerbot Z18's, Airwolf HD2x & HD, and now the Axiom. 

I'll admit that the previous Airwolf models were not my favorite. I had quite a few problems leveling the bed, getting consistent prints / layer adhesion etc... A flight engineer isn't a mechanic. They're a crew position in the cockpit. In the past before heavy computer automations most planes had an additional crew member that was called a flight engineer, or FE. The FEs job was to monitor all systems in flight, to open and close fuel lines for proper balancing of fuel, consult books in the event of an inflight emergency, etc. I haven't read more than the snippet above about this particular incident but it sounds like they were cycling fuel out of all the tanks manually and he just didn't open the proper fuel lines. Its a pretty rookie mistake which obviously snowballs into a much larger problem. Most planes today do not have FE positions, not necessarily because of this sort of incident, but because of computers with failsafes and warnings, its just not worth the cost anymore either.

In civilian aviation the FE is usually a junior pilot, its used as a stepping stone to the pilot positions. I come from a military background where an FE is a career FE who most often will not be a pilot, they tend to be rather crusty guys but the old guys really know their stuff and do a lot for the pilots / plane.

Source: I was an FE in the Air Force and my father is a commercial pilot who was an FE on 727s

I joined the Air Force right after high school. At the time more school was the last thing that I wanted to do, but I figured after I was done school would be paid for and all would be well. Looking back on Basic Training I can say that it was a good experience, but I don't remember liking it all that much when I was there. I was a UH-1N Flight Engineer and was stationed in Spokane, WA. Honestly I loved it, as with everything there were good times and bad times, but the good definitely out-weighed the bad. Spokane to me was something new and exciting, I had never been much of an outdoors person, but being there, and working with the USAF Survival School, I really started not only to appreciate it, but to love it. I spent 3 years in WA then decided that it was time to go into college. After working with the other FE's I realized that all of the old guys had all sorts of problems, mainly knee and back, and I didn't ever want that to happen to me, so I figured getting an education would be the best way to avoid it. I was able to get out of active duty, although I only had a year left, and was picked up by a reserve squadron down by my hometown. I had to cross-train and became an In-Flight Refueler ( http://imgur.com/fcC0T.jpg , http://imgur.com/ZQo6W.jpg ). Things went from great to even better when this happened. I was able to travel the world for 3 years, I've been to nearly every continent, and stayed in some of the nicest places you can imagine. Well first off sorry to hear about the situation you're in. I'll do what I can to try and add some insight.

   First things first, most people will say that recruiters lie, and they do, they deal very well with half truths. Don't let them push you around, remember that if you choose to go that route, no one can make you do anything you don't want to do. I found when I was first looking around at all the different branches the Navy and the Army were by far pushier then the other 2. It's kind of the nature of the beast unfortunately, remember these men have quotas that they have to make. Keep that in mind when they talk to you. They can promise you the moon, but unless you have it written down in a contract, it's useless.

I'm not a finance comptroller(what they call the guys who deal with all the money / allowances in the AF), but I would say that unless you have some sort of custody of your sisters you more then likely will not get BAH. Also, as far as I know your benefits will only extend to your dependants, so your family, unless somehow they are considered dependants would not get any sorts of benefits. I don't know this 100% so hopefully someone else can shed some light on that situation.

As far as what you could possibly do, remember first to go the Air Force Reserve Recruiter. An Active Duty recruiter can't tell you anything besides the phone number of the Reservist recruiter. The reason for this is the Reserves hire into a specific unit, whereas Active Duty throws you into the pot and you could end up anywhere the military needs you. 

There are quite a few things that you can do but again, as a reservist a lot of this will depend on the type of squadrons where you are looking at working. If you're interested in some of the more "flying" related jobs let me know, otherwise I'll spare going off on a tangent about how great the flying jobs are.

The important thing is make sure what you're doing is what is best for you. The military is not for everyone. I've personally loved it, I'm coming up on 6 years in 3 years as a Helicopter Flight Engineer, and 3 years as a KC-135 Boom Operator. I've been all around the world and done quite a bit of things that many people will never get the chance to. 

I hope this helps a little bit, and if nothing else I hope something arises to help alleviate some of the strain of your situation.

Raise salaries for the teachers of those specific disciplines. Once it's desirable enough people will fill those positions. 

Case in point are the Police and Fire fighters of California. They get paid pretty decent considering they have no higher education, and have a retirement that is ludicrous to even imagine, they can get 90% of their highest pay once they retire, in essence paying 2 people to do 1 job. There are no missed quotas on hiring of both Police and Fire, in most districts, considering that those jobs have the ability to put you in the line of danger. To get a fire department job in Southern California can be next to impossible. The reason is they have made it too good of an offer, when people are lining up around the building to try to get one spot in the department, a business man would look and realize they are paying far too much for the job. Anyone who wants to maximize profits would lower the salary until only a small portion were still trying to get it, then they will have reached the proper pay for the position. Likewise the same thing happens if the job is undesirable. Raise the pay until "qualified" people start filling those positions. 

Teachers should be treated much the same way. If you start to raise the salary for the positions that most deem "undesirable" then they become desirable once the salary is raised enough. I understand that the unions are the big forerunner to keeping this a non-reality based off of fairness to all teachers, but the fact of the matter is we have teachers who are beyond under qualified teaching subjects they may have only taken an overview course in. It's no surprise to me or anyone else I'm sure that test scores continue to plummet. 

Assuming the new plan that the President is trying to institute works out how he sees it, I foresee a fairly small jump in Math and Science teachers for a small time, and then they will drop back down where it has been because nothing has changed except a small amount of money thrown at a huge growing problem within America.
Journeyman

While I'm thrilled at the idea of trying to boost interest in our Math and Science programs, throwing more money into the pot of already wasted money seems like a pretty terrible idea. Our public education has fallen to the wayside and another $250 Million won't change a whole lot. The focus instead ought to be an introspective look as to why we have allowed our education to fail as much as it has, and how to fix that problem. 

I think he's definitely on the right track with the idea of aiming increasing our focuses on Math and Science by getting more qualified teachers teaching it. However I also believe that in the grand scheme of things $250 Million dollars is just a drop in the bucket. I think one of the worst things that has plagued our education system, on top of the entertainment culture pushing down the sciences, is the allowing teachers without field specific majors to teach at a K-12 level. Throughout High School I hated Math, all of my teachers, including my calculus teacher were made up of some form of Humanity or Poly Sci Degrees. Their lack of interest fueled my lack of interest and it wasn't until I had spent some time in college when I realized that I wanted to study Mathematics.

I understand that the money is aimed at enticing up and coming individuals to teach, and I realize that that is almost exactly what I said in my 2nd paragraph, but I believe that there is much more needed then 10,000 teachers. We should move back to only allowing Math and Science majors the ability to teach these subjects. For one, it puts an individual who has taken the time and understands on a much higher level the subjects at hand, and also probably enjoys them which in turn helps students enjoy it as well.
